prompt: Which of the three boots a real Android system image, with its own kernel?
hint: Which one is a virtual machine?

choices.text: The iOS Simulator, when it runs an Android app
choices.why: The simulator runs iOS apps, as Mac processes, and boots nothing.

choices.text: The Android emulator
choices.why: Right. It is a virtual machine that boots Google's image on made-up hardware.

choices.text: Android Studio's layout preview
choices.why: The preview draws a layout; it runs no Android at all.

choices.text: A real device, and only that
choices.why: A phone boots its maker's build, but the emulator boots a real image too.

prompt: An app reaches boxoffice at localhost from the iOS Simulator, but needs 10.0.2.2 from the Android emulator. Why the difference?
hint: Which of the two is a machine of its own?

choices.text: Apple configures localhost to mean the Mac as a courtesy to developers
choices.why: Nothing is configured: the app is simply a process on the Mac.

choices.text: iOS forbids 10.0.2.2
choices.why: iOS has no reason to know that address; the simulator never needed one.

choices.text: The emulator is slower to resolve names
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with which machine an address means.

choices.text: One is a process sharing the Mac's network, the other a virtual machine
choices.why: Right. The simulator is the Mac process; inside the emulator, localhost is the emulator, so it gives the computer another address.

prompt: Match each one to what it imitates.
hint: The figure's amber boxes.

pairs.right: the operating system, on the Mac's hardware
nothing: it is true for itself only

right_distractors: the network of a moving train

prompt: The emulator's hardware list declares hw.battery as a boolean, "Whether the device can run on a battery". What does that tell a tester?
hint: What is a yes-or-no able to model?

choices.text: The battery is a switch and a number you set
choices.why: Right. No real battery wears, heats or triggers a maker's power saving.

choices.text: That the emulator measures your laptop's battery and passes it on
choices.why: It declares a battery, it does not read yours; the charge is set by hand.

choices.text: That battery tests cannot be written for Android
choices.why: They can; they just need a phone to mean anything about a phone.

choices.text: That every virtual phone runs on mains power alone
choices.why: The default is yes: the virtual phone has a battery, an imitated one.

prompt: Which of these defects does the emulator show as a user would meet them?
hint: Is the defect in Android and the app, or in the phone and the world?

choices.text: A title cut off when the phone is set to Portuguese
choices.why: Right: language and layout are Android and the app.

choices.text: The denied path of the notification permission
choices.why: Right: the permission system is Android's own.

choices.text: A list that stutters on a cheap phone
choices.why: The emulator has your computer's processor, which hides it.

choices.text: A reminder one brand's battery saver never lets fire
choices.why: The emulator runs Google's Android, with none of that brand's rules.

prompt: Sign-in with Google fails on a new virtual device and works on every phone the team owns. What is the first thing to check?
hint: Where do Google's services come from on an emulator?

choices.text: Whether boxoffice is running
choices.why: Sign-in with Google does not go through boxoffice.

choices.text: Whether the emulator has enough memory
choices.why: Memory would slow it, not remove a service.

choices.text: Whether its system image is a Google APIs one
choices.why: Right. A plain image has no Play services, and the failure is the image's.

choices.text: Whether the phones have a newer Android version than the emulator, since Google sign-in needs the newest
choices.why: Version matters less than whether Play services are present at all.

prompt: An app scans the QR code on a printed ticket. What can the emulator test about it, and what needs a phone?
hint: Which camera modes does the emulator offer?

choices.text: Nothing: the emulator has no camera
choices.why: It has three kinds: a drawn picture, your webcam and a virtual scene.

choices.text: The flow around the scan; how well the lens reads needs a phone
choices.why: Right. Permission, screens and the result are testable here; no emulated camera is the phone's lens.

choices.text: Everything, through the webcam
choices.why: A webcam is your computer's lens, not the phone's, in light that is not a theatre's.

choices.text: Only the reading, since the flow needs real hardware
choices.why: It is the other way round: the flow is software, the reading is hardware.

prompt: In the capture of `emulator -help-gpu`, the mode that uses your computer's own OpenGL driver is called ___.
hint: The opposite of the guest.

prompt: Why can a defect in the file a user installs from the App Store never appear in the simulator?
hint: What is the simulator's binary built for?

choices.text: Because the simulator runs an older iOS
choices.why: It runs whichever iOS version you pick; the build is the issue.

choices.text: It runs a build for the Mac's processor
choices.why: Right. The phone's binary is compiled again, for the phone, and signed.

choices.text: Because App Store apps are encrypted against simulators
choices.why: The point is earlier: the simulator never had that binary to run.

choices.text: Because the simulator has no network
choices.why: It has the Mac's network, which is why localhost worked in lesson 18.

prompt: An iPhone 11 closes the app while a long list loads. In the simulator the same list loads fine. What explains the difference?
hint: Whose memory does the simulator use?

choices.text: The simulator's iOS is a different version
choices.why: Even the same version would not close it: the limit is the phone's.

choices.text: The phone's network is slower
choices.why: A slow network delays the list; it does not close the app.

choices.text: It has the Mac's memory
choices.why: Right, and no phone's limit. iOS on an older phone closes an app that uses too much; on the Mac nothing does.

choices.text: XCUITest closes apps that take long
choices.why: No test was involved; a person saw it on the phone.

prompt: Where does the section send you for the list of hardware and frameworks the simulator lacks?
hint: The list changes, so where is it current?

choices.text: To a table in this course, which is the final word
choices.why: The list changes with every Xcode, so a course cannot be the final word.

choices.text: To the Android emulator's hardware list
choices.why: That describes the emulator, not Apple's simulator.

choices.text: To the App Store reviews of the app
choices.why: Reviews describe the app, not the simulator.

choices.text: Apple's own documentation
choices.why: Right: its Simulator documentation, read for the Xcode version you use, since the list changes with every one.

prompt: Match each defect to where it can be seen.
hint: The rows of the table.

pairs.left: a wrong field from the API on screen
a reminder that never fires on one brand
pairs.right: only on a phone of that brand

pairs.left: slow scrolling on a cheap phone
a request failing when the network drops
pairs.right: on all three, once set up

prompt: A manager asks whether the release "works on real devices". What does the section suggest asking instead?
hint: A question that has one answer.

choices.text: Whether it works on the newest iPhone and the newest Pixel
choices.why: That names two devices, not the defect anybody fears.

choices.text: Which defect, exactly, we fear
choices.why: Right. A named defect has a place in the table; 'real devices' in general has none.

choices.text: How many phones the team owns
choices.why: A count says nothing about which defects they could show.

choices.text: Whether the emulator tests passed
choices.why: They answer the first rows of the table, not the device-only ones.

prompt: Which adb command reads the exact build of the maker's Android off a connected phone?
hint: The last of the four.

choices.text: adb shell getprop ro.product.model
choices.why: That is the model, which many builds share.

choices.text: adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release
choices.why: That is the Android version, such as 14, not the maker's build of it.

choices.text: adb shell getprop ro.build.fingerprint
choices.why: Right. It names the maker's exact build.

choices.text: adb devices
choices.why: That lists serial numbers, not builds.

prompt: A user reports that the list stutters on a Moto E with Android 12. An emulator with Android 12 and the same screen scrolls smoothly. What do you conclude?
hint: Which row of the table is this?

choices.text: That it cannot be reproduced, so the report can be closed
choices.why: It cannot be reproduced where the defect is hidden; that is not the same thing.

choices.text: That the user's phone is faulty
choices.why: Possible, but slow scrolling on a cheap phone is a known class the emulator hides.

choices.text: That Android 12 is to blame, so test on Android 13
choices.why: The emulator had Android 12 and was smooth; the version is not the difference.

choices.text: It sits in a row the emulator hides; try that phone
choices.why: Right. On a shelf or in a device cloud, and write down where it did and did not reproduce.

prompt: A user reports a defect from a phone you do not have. Put the section's steps in order.
hint: Cheapest first.
items: read the report for maker, model, version and language
try an emulator set up like that phone
find that model, or the nearest one, in a device cloud
write down where it reproduced and where it did not

prompt: Why does the shelf include the oldest supported Android version, on a cheap phone of your users' commonest brand?
hint: What does that one phone find that the emulator hides?

choices.text: It finds the emulator's blind spots, for most users
choices.why: Right: slow screens, memory limits and the brand's background rules, on the phone most of your users resemble.

choices.text: Because old phones are cheaper to replace when tests break them
choices.why: Tests do not break phones; the choice is about what the phone reveals.

choices.text: Because the emulator cannot run old Android versions
choices.why: It runs any version you download; it cannot run a cheap phone's hardware.

choices.text: Because new phones are not allowed in test labs
choices.why: The shelf has a recent phone too, of another brand.

prompt: After every escaped defect, a team buys the phone it was reported from. Three years on they own twenty. What does the section say is wrong with that?
hint: Chosen by whom, for what?

choices.text: Twenty is too few; a team needs one of every model
choices.why: Nobody can own every model; that is what renting is for.

choices.text: Phones bought after a defect are always faulty
choices.why: Nothing makes those phones faulty; they are just chosen by accident.

choices.text: They were chosen by accident, nobody keeps them up, and the next user's model is still missing
choices.why: Right. Three chosen from your own users beat twenty chosen this way.

choices.text: Real phones should not be used at all once there is an emulator
choices.why: The section keeps a shelf; it only asks that it be chosen.

prompt: In the section's plan, which place runs the automated suites on every change?
hint: The cheapest.

choices.text: The shelf of real phones, by hand
choices.why: A person uses those before a release; they are too slow for every change.

choices.text: Emulators and simulators
choices.why: Right: cheap, quick, and resetting in a second.

choices.text: A device cloud
choices.why: That runs every night or before a release, because it costs by the minute.

choices.text: The users' own phones
choices.why: Users are not a test suite.

prompt: The budget pays for one real Android phone. Analytics say most users are on budget Samsung phones with Android 12 and 13, and the app supports Android 12 and later. Which phone?
hint: The first phone of the shelf.

choices.text: The newest Pixel, because it gets Android updates first
choices.why: It runs Google's Android on fast hardware: what the emulator already shows.

choices.text: A cheap one of that brand, on version 12
choices.why: Right: the oldest supported version, on your users' commonest brand and price.

choices.text: A premium Samsung on the newest Android
choices.why: Right brand, wrong hardware and version: it hides the slow screens your users meet.

choices.text: None: spend it on the device cloud for one month instead
choices.why: A cloud covers the long tail; a phone at hand covers the journeys a person must touch.

prompt: A reminder fires on the emulator and on the shelf's Samsung, and never on a Xiaomi in the device cloud. How should it be written up?
hint: Is it a defect if only one brand's users meet it?

choices.text: Not at all: it is the brand's fault, not the app's
choices.why: Users of that brand still lose their reminder; a defect is what a user meets.

choices.text: As a defect on that brand, with maker, model, version and fingerprint, saying it passes elsewhere
choices.why: Right. Where it fails and where it passes is the evidence the developers need.

choices.text: As a flaky test, to be retried until it passes
choices.why: It fails every time on one brand; that is not flakiness.

choices.text: As a defect in the device cloud
choices.why: The cloud showed a real phone's behaviour; that is its job.

prompt: An iOS team tested only on the simulator. The first build sent to testers will not install on anyone's iPhone. Which row of the table is this, and why did nothing warn them?
hint: What does a phone check that the simulator does not?

choices.text: A memory limit, which the simulator hides
choices.why: Memory limits close a running app; this one never installed.

choices.text: A layout on a small screen
choices.why: A layout defect shows after installing, and the simulator shows it.

choices.text: Plain HTTP refused
choices.why: That blocks a request inside a running app, on the simulator too.

choices.text: A build signed wrong
choices.why: Right. The simulator checks no provisioning, so the phone is the first place that checks the signature.
